passage: Eshaan and Tejas had traded first and second rank at their Pune engineering college since the first semester, and everyone in the lab knew it. The night before the robotics demo, Eshaan found Tejas's team notebook left open on the shared bench, with the password for their test rig written on the cover. For a long moment he just looked at it. One changed line and their robot would stall in front of the judges. Instead he closed the notebook and texted Tejas: 'You left your stuff on bench 3. Password's on the cover, might want to hide it.' Then he went back to his own robot and rewrote the turning function a third time, because Tejas's arm had looked smoother than his in the trial. At the demo, Tejas's team won by two points. Eshaan shook his hand and asked how they had tuned the arm.

qa.q: On which bench did Tejas leave the notebook?
qa.a: Tejas left the notebook on bench 3.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling as he looked at the open notebook?
qa.a: Eshaan felt tempted and tense, the rivalry pulling toward sabotage, before he chose to close it.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Warning Tejas and putting the energy into his own turning function, because it kept him decent and actually raised his standard.

qa.q: How might Tejas see Eshaan's text about the notebook?
qa.a: Tejas would likely be surprised and grateful, seeing his rival as someone who competes fairly.

grounding: Shows a long rivalry where the temptation to sabotage is refused and the rival instead pushes Eshaan to improve his own work.

passage:
'Just shelve the constitutional law volume in the wrong section,' Anmol whispered. 'Disha needs it tonight for her memorial.'
'No.'
'Dhruv, she beat you in the last two moots.'
'I know exactly how many times she beat me.' Dhruv pulled the volume off the shelf himself. 'Which is why I'm reading it first, properly. Then I'm putting it back.'
Later, at the library door, Disha caught up with him. 'Heard you were in the reference section for three hours.'
'Couldn't let you walk in with better arguments again.'
She laughed. 'Your rebuttal last time was good, by the way. I stole the structure.'
'Then I'm stealing your opening. Fair?'
'Fair. See you Friday.'
Anmol shook his head. 'You two are strange.'
'She makes me better,' Dhruv said. 'That's the whole point of her.'

qa.q: What did Anmol suggest doing with the volume?
qa.a: Anmol suggested shelving it in the wrong section.

qa.q: How does Dhruv feel about Disha beating him?
qa.a: Dhruv feels stung and competitive, keeping count of every loss, but he respects her and wants to beat her fairly.

qa.q: What would you advise someone tempted the way Dhruv was?
qa.a: Refuse the sabotage and put the energy into preparing better, as Dhruv did by reading the volume first and putting it back.

qa.q: How does Disha seem to see the rivalry?
qa.a: Disha treats it as friendly and useful, openly borrowing Dhruv's rebuttal structure and laughing about it.

grounding: Shows a rival refusing a friend's sabotage idea and using the competition to lift his own preparation while staying decent.

passage: The rumour reached Shankar on the morning of the final placement round: that he had made the shortlist because his uncle knew the company's HR head. He had forty minutes before his interview, and the batch group chat was buzzing with it. His first instinct was to post a furious reply naming who he thought had started it, probably Kashish, who had been cut from the same shortlist. He didn't. He had no proof and no time. Instead he found the placement coordinator and said calmly, 'There's a story going round that my shortlisting was fixed. Please check my test scores and the process. I'd like it on record.' The coordinator nodded and pulled up the sheet. Then Shankar walked into the interview and answered every question as well as he could. By evening the coordinator had posted the shortlist criteria for the whole batch. Shankar never replied in the group.

qa.q: How long did Shankar have before his interview?
qa.a: Shankar had forty minutes before his interview.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when he first heard the rumour?
qa.a: Shankar felt angry and wronged, wanting to post a furious reply naming someone.

qa.q: What went right in how Shankar handled the rumour?
qa.a: He calmly went to the key person, the placement coordinator, asked for a check on record, and let his interview speak for him.

qa.q: What would change if Shankar had posted the furious reply naming Kashish?
qa.a: It could have started a second rumour, possibly unfair to Kashish, and made Shankar look guilty just before the interview.

grounding: Shows a false story spreading under time pressure, and Shankar calmly going to the key person instead of chasing whispers or hitting back.

passage: By Wednesday the whole theatre club in Kolkata seemed to have heard it: Sabina had got the lead in the spring play only because she was 'close' to Hrithik, the student director. She wasn't; they had barely spoken outside rehearsals. Her roommate showed her a screenshot of someone's story with a winking caption. Sabina's hands shook. She thought about posting something nasty about the girl who had lost the role. Instead, she did three things. She told Hrithik quietly, so he wouldn't be blindsided. She asked the faculty advisor, who had sat on the audition panel, to explain how casting was decided at the next meeting. And she stopped opening screenshots. At Friday's rehearsal she was first to arrive and knew every line of Act Two. The whispers thinned. Nobody apologised, but within a week people had moved on to something else.

qa.q: What role did Hrithik have in the club?
qa.a: Hrithik was the student director.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when her roommate showed her the screenshot?
qa.a: Sabina felt shaken and angry, her hands trembling, and was tempted to post something nasty back.

qa.q: What did Sabina get right?
qa.a: She calmly told the key people, Hrithik and the faculty advisor, stopped chasing screenshots, and let her work at rehearsal speak.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel being warned by Sabina?
qa.a: Hrithik would probably feel grateful not to be blindsided, and could back the casting process instead of reacting in surprise.

grounding: Shows a false story about how a role was won, and Sabina speaking calmly to the people who matter and letting her conduct answer the whispers.

passage: Vinita's first month in Gurugram followed a pattern. Office till seven, a shared cab, then a rented room with a fan that ticked. The evenings sat on her like a wet blanket. She ate dinner in front of her phone, scrolling her sister's photos from home in Indore, the cousins on the terrace, Mummy's kadhi in a steel bowl, until it was midnight and she felt worse. On a Sunday she wrote a short list on the back of a bill: walk to the park every evening at 7:30; badminton club on Tuesdays and Thursdays; call home after dinner, not during. The first Tuesday was awkward. She missed most shots. A colleague from accounts, Pradeep, was there too and said, 'Next time, doubles?' It wasn't a friendship yet. But the walk home felt shorter, and she stopped expecting it all to be fixed by next week.

qa.q: On which days does the badminton club meet?
qa.a: The badminton club meets on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling after scrolling her sister's photos?
qa.a: Vinita felt lonely and homesick, worse than before, with the evenings weighing on her.

qa.q: Which small steps helped Vinita's evenings?
qa.a: An evening walk, joining the badminton club, and calling home after dinner instead of scrolling through it.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Vinita at the first badminton evening?
qa.a: Pradeep likely sees a new colleague finding her feet and offers doubles as an easy way to include her.

grounding: Shows heavy, lonely evenings in a new city and the slow fix of routines, a club, and accepting that friendship takes time.

passage:
'You sound flat, Asif. What did you do today?'
'Work. Came back. Lay on the bed.'
'And yesterday?'
'Same. Scrolled everyone's photos from the wedding I missed.'
'Man, you've been in Chennai two months. What's around you?'
'A tea stall. A gym I pay for and don't go to. A running group that meets on the beach on Sundays, I think.'
'Go to the running group.'
'I don't know anyone.'
'That's literally why you go.'
'It'll take forever to make friends here, Tarun.'
'Yeah. Months, probably. So start the clock. And go to the gym on your way home, same time every day, so it's a habit, not a decision.'
Asif was quiet, then laughed a little. 'You're very bossy on the phone.'
'Send me a photo from the beach on Sunday.'
On Sunday a blurry photo arrived: sand, twelve runners, and Asif's thumb.

qa.q: Where does the running group meet?
qa.a: The running group meets on the beach on Sundays.

qa.q: What does Asif's flat voice suggest about how Asif feels?
qa.a: It suggests Asif is lonely and low, withdrawing to bed and scrolling after two months in a new city.

qa.q: What advice from Tarun is most useful, and why?
qa.a: Going to the gym at the same time daily and joining the running group, because routines and regular groups slowly build ties.

qa.q: What is it like for Tarun hearing Asif sound so flat?
qa.a: Tarun is concerned, and pushes kindly with plans and a photo request so Asif doesn't keep withdrawing.

grounding: Shows loneliness after a move, with withdrawing and scrolling, and a friend nudging toward routines, a group and patience.

passage:
Week 1: In her Kolkata PG, Jahnavi ate the mess rice in silence and counted the days until the Dussehra break, when she would go home to Mysuru. Every night she called Amma and cried quietly once the Kannada greetings started.
Week 3: The cook put mustard in everything. Jahnavi found a small tiffin place near the metro run by a man named Jeevan, who turned out to be from Mangaluru. He spoke to her in Kannada and gave extra chutney. She started going every Saturday morning.
Week 6: She still called home every night, but the calls were shorter. On Saturdays she brought her roommate Rupsa to Jeevan's for dosa, and Rupsa taught her three Bengali phrases in return. The Dussehra ticket was still booked. She just wasn't counting days anymore.

qa.q: Where was Jeevan from?
qa.a: Jeevan was from Mangaluru.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling in Week 1 when the Kannada greetings started?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt homesick and lonely, missing her language and family enough to cry quietly.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see Jahnavi's Saturday visits?
qa.a: Jeevan probably enjoys meeting a fellow Kannada speaker far from home, which is why he chats and adds extra chutney.

grounding: Shows homesickness for food and language easing as Jahnavi keeps calling home but builds small anchors in the new city.

passage: Asif, you keep checking train tickets on your lunch break in this canteen. I know that look; I'm Leela, and thirty years ago I had it worse. I came from Thrissur to Delhi at twenty-one for my first job. I hated the rotis, I hated the cold, and nobody said my name the way my mother did. For eight months I lived for the train home. I saved every leave, skipped every office picnic, spent Sundays in my room with Malayalam songs. And every time I came back from Thrissur it hurt more, because nothing here was mine. Then a Tamil lady in my building asked if I wanted to share a rice cooker. We cooked sambar together every Sunday. I joined her temple choir. The train stayed, but it stopped being my whole life. So call home, Asif. And also find your rice cooker.

qa.q: Where did Leela move from, and at what age?
qa.a: Leela came from Thrissur to Delhi at twenty-one.

qa.q: What was young Leela feeling each time she came back from Thrissur?
qa.a: Leela felt more homesick and hollow each time, because nothing in Delhi felt like Leela's own.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Leela settle?
qa.a: Saying yes to sharing a rice cooker with the neighbour, then Sunday sambar and the choir, which gave Leela anchors in Delhi.

qa.q: How might the neighbour have felt offering to share the rice cooker?
qa.a: The neighbour, perhaps also far from home, may have wanted company and someone to cook with on Sundays.

grounding: An older colleague recalls living only for trips home, and how small anchors in the new city eased the homesickness.

passage: Friday night. Diary, Rashmi reporting: I finally said more than 'hi' to the man across the corridor. For six weeks I've heard Ramesh's pressure cooker whistle at 8 every evening and wondered if he's as alone in this building as I am. I kept waiting for him to knock. He didn't. Tonight I had extra lemon pickle from home, so I knocked instead, heart going like a drum. He looked surprised, then pleased. We talked for four minutes about the water timings and the lift that's always broken. That's all. But on Monday I'll ask if he knows a good vegetable vendor, and maybe on Wednesday I'll say hi at the gate without rehearsing it first. Small and repeated, that's the plan. Awkward is fine. Awkward is better than another silent week.

qa.q: At what time does Ramesh's pressure cooker whistle?
qa.a: Ramesh's pressure cooker whistles at 8 every evening.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling while knocking on the door?
qa.a: Rashmi felt nervous, heart going like a drum, but hopeful enough to knock.

qa.q: What is Rashmi's plan, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Small repeated contacts, like asking about a vegetable vendor on Monday and saying hi at the gate, because friendship grows through many short meetings.

qa.q: How might Ramesh have felt when Rashmi knocked?
qa.a: Ramesh looked surprised, then pleased, perhaps glad that someone in the building reached out first.

grounding: A diary shows the fear of awkwardness with a neighbour and the choice to stop waiting and build contact through small repeated steps.

passage: Francis, before you pay that broker, listen to your Yogesh-uncle's foolishness. I was twenty, new in Mumbai, and a landlord in Dadar offered me a room with a handshake. 'Why paper between us?' he said, and I felt grown-up saying yes. Three months later he doubled the rent and said the deposit was 'for damages'. There were no damages. I had nothing written, no neighbour's number, nobody I had asked. Worst of all, I told my father everything was fine. For weeks I ate one meal a day and lied on every phone call. It was a senior at work, Mr. D'Souza, who noticed and took me to the tenants' office, where someone explained what I should have had in writing. After that I told my father the truth. He wasn't angry. So: paper first, numbers saved, and call your mother tonight.

qa.q: Where was the landlord's room?
qa.a: The room was in Dadar.

qa.q: How did young Yogesh feel during the weeks he lied on phone calls?
qa.a: Yogesh felt ashamed and alone, hiding the trouble from his father while barely eating.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things for Yogesh?

qa.q: How might Yogesh's father have felt on finally hearing the truth?
qa.a: His father wasn't angry, and was probably sorry to have been kept out of the trouble for so long.

passage: The rain had knocked out power across the lane in Hyderabad when Jahnavi came back to her PG and found her room unlocked. The owner's husband was inside with a torch, 'checking the fan'. Nobody had asked her. It was the second time. She stood in the doorway, dripping, until he left. Her rent terms were a single spoken promise, and when she had asked for them in writing, the owner had laughed. Tonight her phone was at eight percent. She called Madhuri, a senior from her college who had lived in the area for two years. 'Come to my place tonight,' Madhuri said. 'Tomorrow we go together and ask for a written agreement and your own key, or we find you another PG. And call your parents.' Jahnavi hesitated; she hadn't wanted to worry them. Then, under Madhuri's umbrella at the auto stand, she dialled home.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi's phone battery at?
qa.a: Jahnavi's phone was at eight percent.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling standing dripping in the doorway?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt unsafe and shaken, finding someone in her room without permission for the second time.

qa.q: Which steps made Jahnavi safer?
qa.a: Going to Madhuri's for the night, planning to ask for a written agreement and her own key or move out, and calling her parents.

qa.q: Why might Jahnavi's parents want to hear about this tonight?
qa.a: They would rather know and help plan than be kept in the dark, even if the news worries them.

grounding: Shows a newcomer made vulnerable by unclear rental terms, and the wise response of calling a senior, seeking terms in writing and telling family.

passage: Honestly, in my first year in Bhopal, my closest friends were four people I'd never met. I'm Kalyani, by the way, and I'm not embarrassed about it. Every night at ten we'd log on to the same strategy game, and Simran, who lives in Nagpur, would say 'report, Captain' in a silly voice until I laughed. When I had a fever, it was the team that sent me soup through a food-delivery app. They were real to me. But one Saturday I realised I hadn't spoken out loud to anyone in my own city for three days. Not the security guard, not my classmates. That scared me a little. So I kept the ten o'clock games, and I also joined the college astronomy club on Fridays. Simran was the one who pushed me: 'Go look at real stars, Captain.' Now I have both. I still log on. I also know the guard's name.

qa.q: Where does Simran live?
qa.a: Simran lives in Nagpur.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel on realising three days had passed without speaking aloud?
qa.a: Kalyani felt a little scared, uneasy at how cut off life in the city had become.

qa.q: What balance did Kalyani find?
qa.a: Keeping the ten o'clock games while joining the astronomy club on Fridays, so online friends did not replace in-person ones.

qa.q: How does Simran seem to see Kalyani joining the club?
qa.a: Simran is supportive rather than jealous, even pushing Kalyani to 'go look at real stars'.

grounding: A spoken account values online friends while noticing they had replaced all in-person contact, and adding a real-world club.

passage: Mei told her mother on every call that uni in Melbourne was 'great, so busy'. It wasn't. Five weeks in, she ate lunch on the library steps, watching groups laughing on the lawn, sure that everyone else had found their people in week one. She had even posted a photo of a crowded party she'd walked past, as if she had been inside. In Thursday's tutorial, Yara, who always sat by the door, asked if she wanted to grab a coffee. Mei nearly said she was busy. Then, halfway through the coffee, she said something she hadn't planned: 'Honestly, I don't really know anyone here yet.' Yara put down her cup. 'Me neither. Some days I've eaten lunch in the bathroom.' They both laughed, a little shocked. The next Thursday they sat together, and Mei called her mother and said, 'It's hard, actually.'

qa.q: Where did Mei eat lunch?
qa.a: Mei ate lunch on the library steps.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling as she watched the groups on the lawn?
qa.a: Mei felt lonely and ashamed, sure everyone else had found friends in week one.

qa.q: How does Yara respond to Mei's honesty, and why?
qa.a: Yara seems relieved enough to admit being lonely too, even eating lunch in the bathroom some days.

grounding: Shows the belief that everyone else has friends, the cover-up of pretending, and one honest conversation revealing the feeling is shared.

passage: The notice board in the trainees' common room at the nursing college in Kochi was full of photos: Onam celebrations, group trips, birthday cakes. Neelam wasn't in any of them. Two months in, she smiled in class, answered every question and told everyone she was 'totally settled'. At night she walked the corridor so she wouldn't have to sit alone in her room. One evening the warden's assistant, Sangeeta, found her there at eleven. 'You walk here a lot,' Sangeeta said, not unkindly. Neelam started to say she was fine, and then didn't. 'I think everyone here has friends except me.' Sangeeta sat on the bench. 'I counted once. Half the trainees in this block tell me that in their first term.' Neelam laughed in disbelief. Sangeeta pointed at the board. 'Photos don't show who went home and cried.' The next week, Neelam signed up for the block's Sunday cooking rota.

qa.q: What did the photos on the notice board show?
qa.a: The photos showed Onam celebrations, group trips and birthday cakes.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling while walking the corridor at night?

qa.q: What helped Neelam move past pretending?
qa.a: Admitting the truth to Sangeeta and then joining the Sunday cooking rota.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see Neelam's loneliness?
qa.a: Sangeeta sees it as very common, hearing the same thing from half the trainees in the block in their first term.

grounding: Shows a trainee pretending to be settled while ashamed of being lonely, and one honest talk showing that many feel the same.

passage: Neelam, you said no to the canteen group again today; I saw. Let Trisha-aunty tell you a small thing. My first job was at a bank branch in Pune, forty years ago. A colleague named Rosy asked me to lunch on my second day. I said I'd brought tiffin. She asked the next week; I said I was tired. She asked a third time; I said maybe tomorrow, and hid in the record room. After a month she stopped asking. I ate alone for most of that year. Then one Friday I was so tired I nearly said no again, but I said yes just to stop myself. We ate vada pav on the steps. Rosy became the friend who carried my wedding sari and held my first baby. All from one tired yes. So tomorrow, when they ask, say yes, Neelam.

qa.a: They ate vada pav on the steps.

qa.q: How might young Trisha have felt hiding in the record room?
qa.a: Trisha was likely shy and anxious, avoiding the lunch even though it left her eating alone.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Trisha's first year?
qa.a: Saying yes to Rosy on a tired Friday, which began a lifelong friendship.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Rosy when Trisha kept saying no?
qa.a: Rosy may have felt turned away and unsure whether Trisha wanted company, which is why she stopped asking after a month.

grounding: An aunt recalls declining a colleague's lunch invitations out of shyness, and how one tired yes began a lifelong friendship.

passage: It was pouring over Whitefield, Vishal had just finished a ten-hour shift fixing a server crash, and all he wanted was his bed. Then Sahil from the next desk leaned over. 'A few of us are getting biryani near the metro. Come?' Vishal had said no twice already that month: once for laundry, once because he didn't know anyone and the thought of small talk made his stomach tight. He opened his mouth to say 'next time'. Instead he heard himself say, 'Okay, give me five minutes.' The biryani place was loud and the auto ride was wet. He barely spoke for the first half hour. Then someone asked about his hometown, Jalandhar, and Sahil turned out to have cousins there. They shared an auto back. On Monday, Sahil saved him a chair at lunch.

passage: Yusuf had come to Serchhip, a small town in Mizoram, for a year-long rural teaching fellowship. By the seventh week he was falling asleep at 2 a.m. and waking tired, skipping the evening walk to the market, eating biscuits for dinner. He told himself it was the hills, the rain, the language. One evening his landlady's daughter, Lalremsiami, who taught at the same school, found him on the steps staring at nothing. 'You look far away these days,' she said. He almost said he was fine. Then he listed it aloud: bad sleep, no energy, no one to talk to for weeks. Saying it made it sound like a pattern, not a mood. That night he called his mother in Lucknow, and the next morning he emailed the fellowship's counsellor to book a call. On Sunday he went with Lalremsiami's family to their church lunch, though he wasn't a churchgoer.

qa.q: How long was Yusuf's fellowship?
qa.a: It was a year-long rural teaching fellowship.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling by the seventh week?
qa.a: Yusuf felt low, lonely and drained, sleeping badly and losing interest in the market walk.

qa.q: What steps did Yusuf take once he saw the pattern?
qa.a: He called his mother, booked a call with the fellowship's counsellor, and joined Lalremsiami's family for Sunday lunch.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see Yusuf on the steps?
qa.a: Lalremsiami notices he seems far away and cares enough to say so gently.

grounding: Shows weeks of isolation draining sleep and energy, and Yusuf naming the pattern and reaching out to family, a counsellor and neighbours.

passage: By February the Montreal winter had been dark for weeks, and Sami had stopped going to his morning lectures. He slept badly, woke at noon, and told himself there was no point fixing anything; he just wasn't built for this place. On Sunday his older sister Layla video-called from Casablanca, as she did every week. She looked at his face and put her tea down. 'How long has it been like this?' 'A month, maybe more. Nothing helps.' 'What have you tried?' He thought about it. Nothing. He hadn't told anyone. Layla stayed on the call while he opened the university wellness page and booked the first counselling slot, Tuesday at ten. 'And tomorrow you go to one lecture,' she said. 'Just one. Then text me.' On Monday a message reached Casablanca: a photo of a half-empty lecture hall and a thumbs-up.

qa.q: When was the counselling slot Sami booked?
qa.a: The slot was Tuesday at ten.

qa.q: What was Sami feeling before Layla's call?
qa.a: Sami felt hopeless and worn out, sleeping badly and believing nothing would help.

qa.q: What did Layla do that helped Sami move?
qa.a: She asked what he had tried, stayed on the call while he booked counselling, and set one small goal: one lecture.

qa.q: What was it like for Layla to see Sami's face on the call?
qa.a: Layla was worried enough to put her tea down and ask how long it had been going on.

grounding: Shows isolation draining sleep and energy with the belief that nothing will help, and family helping Sami reach a campus counsellor.
